source.title: Spectral Signatures of Data Quality: Eigenvalue Tail Index as a Diagnostic for Label Noise in Neural Networks

page_placements.theme: Spectral and effective-complexity diagnostics are conditional

record.tranche_reason: Measures trained networks’ spectral properties against generalization outcomes using controlled label-noise and hyperparameter sweeps, a different measurement approach that bears on V7’s gap-tracking claim. It also reports generalization and memorization outcomes relevant to V1, but those are comparisons in the supplied version’s domain.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the study’s own comparisons of real versus shuffled labels, spectral observables, controlled noise levels, hyperparameter variation, and CIFAR-10N noise detection. Cited prior-work results are excluded. Values from flattened tables are recorded only where the supplied layout supports assignment; detailed architecture-dependent results on page 3 are cut off mid-description.
record.test_reason: The study tests V1 in a new setting: the same MLP/MNIST recipe achieves >99% training accuracy with natural and random labels, but test accuracy is 98.3% and 9.9%, respectively. Its spectral predictors do not test V7's magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors frame bottleneck tail index as a diagnostic of label corruption and data quality, with strong prediction under label-noise variation but weak prediction under hyperparameter variation. They also conclude that level spacing is uninformative.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures spectral properties and their predictive association with test accuracy under controlled label noise and hyperparameter variation; it does not reproduce the original magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: Predictive strength changes with perturbation axis: tail α is highly predictive under label-noise variation and weak under hyperparameter variation. The Hill estimate varies with threshold quantile q ∈ [0.70, 0.95]. The authors also report that the useful measurement layer varies by architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 21 noise levels, bottleneck tail index predicts test accuracy with LOO R2=0.984; effective rank reaches 0.750 and the best conventional norm baseline reaches 0.149.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Bottleneck spectral shape predicts test accuracy under controlled label corruption better than the tested norm summaries.

fits_no_version.finding: Under clean-label hyperparameter variation, tail-index prediction is weak (R2=0.167), with global L2 norm slightly stronger (0.219).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Spectral prediction depends on the perturbation axis and does not transfer reliably from label corruption to hyperparameter variation.

fits_no_version.finding: CNN outlier fractions differ between natural and random labels; tail-index estimates also vary with the estimator threshold.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Spectral diagnostics depend on layer choice and estimator configuration.

fits_no_version.finding: Level spacing remains near 0.53 for initialization, natural-label training and random-label training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Level spacing does not distinguish memorization from generalization in these weight matrices.

fits_no_version.finding: Synthetic-noise calibration estimates CIFAR-10N annotation noise with reported errors of 3% and 9% for aggregate and worst-annotator labels.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight spectra can estimate dataset-level annotation corruption, with poorer transfer at high class-dependent noise.

record.problems: The evidence uses small-scale MLP, CNN, and ResNet-18 models and standard benchmarks; the authors say scaling to large language models and vision transformers is open. No formal generalization bound is proved; the theoretical framework is heuristic. The Hill estimator has moderate threshold sensitivity and requires roughly 50 eigenvalues for stability. Reported architecture-specific comparison details on page 3 are cut off in the supplied text. Several reported predictive R2 values use seed-averaged data; numerical error bars are not provided in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible results were omitted. Table II's 6-noise-level architecture fits are summarized in Table III's definitive 21-level result and not added as duplicate rows. The paper's level-spacing result is described under fits_no_version; Table I reports its values but those do not measure V1's or V7's named outcome.

untested.parts: The named CIFAR-10/ImageNet architectures and recipes are not reproduced. CNN training interpolation is reported, but paired numerical test accuracies are unavailable.
Test-error trends beyond the width required for interpolation.
Matched convolutional-versus-fully-connected generalization and the role of local connectivity.
Adaptive-versus-SGD held-out performance under specified tuning budgets.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
The entire magnitude-aware perturbation-sharpness claim, including gap correlations and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Remove the V7 verdict: evidence about spectral predictors cannot qualify a claim specifically about magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness. Width and weight-decay sweeps alone do not test V2 or V6. The supplied text contains the continuation of the CNN FC-layer discussion, contrary to the record's truncation claim.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test the named Zhang et al. architectures and recipes; the reported random-label comparison is MLP/MNIST, with additional architecture-specific spectral descriptions.

Does not test the specific magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness measure or compare it with the norm- and margin-based measures in V7. Instead, it evaluates tail index and other spectral observables as predictors under controlled label-noise and hyperparameter variation.

relation.reason: Its own results directly demonstrate V1's coexistence of random-label fitting capacity and natural-label generalization.

tranche.reason: The matched natural/random-label experiment extends V1 to MLP/MNIST, reporting both training fit and held-out accuracy.

source_check.notes: The paper calls random-label replacement shuffling, but its protocol replaces labels uniformly at random; the 10% chance reference is inferred from ten classes, not explicitly reported. The authors-conclusion paraphrase is accurate; spectral prediction measures do not test V7's magnitude-aware sharpness or generalization-gap ranking.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Tail-index prediction under label-noise variation versus hyperparameter variation
reader_labels.reason: Tail α predicts test accuracy strongly across noise levels (R5), but weakly under clean-label hyperparameter variation and is surpassed by global L2 norm (R12, R14). The study does not test magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness itself.
